claims.text: The starting nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
High-temperature exposure causes thermodynamically driven surface segregation of one or more constituent elements.
Oxidizing environments enhance surface segregation relative to inert environments.
Surface segregation initiates the formation of secondary phases.
Surface-driven chemical inhomogeneity governs eventual structural and chemical instability of the nanoparticles.
Varying oxygen partial pressure at elevated temperature while mapping local composition can isolate the effect of reactive atmosphere on segregation.
Surface segregation produces local compositional inhomogeneities followed by nucleation of secondary phases at the nanoparticle surface.
Elevated temperature promotes segregation because selected elements can reduce the nanoparticle surface energy by enriching at the surface.
Less-noble or more-reactive elements are the constituents most likely to segregate.
Oxygen accelerates segregation and causes local oxidation.
Local oxidation produces secondary phases that compromise overall nanoparticle stability.
At high temperature, oxidizing conditions will yield more surface segregation and secondary-phase formation than an inert baseline.
Under inert conditions, the nanoparticles will retain a more homogeneous composition and stable morphology, with minimal segregation and no significant secondary-phase formation.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant between 773 and 1173 K for catalytic service and up to approximately 1200 K for the proposed thermoelectric testing.
Substantial changes in composition or particle size may place the nanoparticles outside the hypothesis's applicability.
Bulk diffusion-induced coarsening could be an alternative contributor to instability.
The temperature and oxygen-concentration thresholds for pronounced segregation and phase formation are not established.
A lack of statistically significant increases in surface segregation or secondary-phase nucleation under oxidizing conditions relative to inert conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
